Westminster Confession of Faith
WEST-min-ster kuhn-FESH-uhn uhv FAYTH
noun (confessional standard)
From Westminster, where the Assembly met in the Abbey's Jerusalem Chamber (1643–49), + confession (Latin confiteri, to acknowledge openly); the Reformed creed it produced.

Biblical Definition

The Westminster Confession of Faith is the confession of faith drawn up by the Westminster Assembly of Divines between 1643 and 1649, the high-water mark of English-speaking Reformed theology. Summoned by the Long Parliament and aided by Scottish commissioners, some hundred and twenty ministers and learned men labored in the Jerusalem Chamber to frame a confession, two catechisms (Larger and Shorter), a Directory for Public Worship, and a Form of Church Government. The Confession opens, unlike the medieval church, not with the church or the sacraments but with Holy Scripture — its sufficiency, authority, and clarity — and proceeds through the decree of God, creation, providence, the fall, the covenant of grace, Christ the Mediator, effectual calling, justification, adoption, sanctification, and the perseverance of the saints, to the last judgment. Its theology is thoroughly Calvinistic and covenantal. The Shorter Catechism's first question — man's chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy Him forever — has catechized generations. This dictionary's own confession, the 1689 London Baptist Confession, deliberately followed Westminster nearly word for word, departing only on baptism, the church, and the civil magistrate. To honor Westminster is to honor the parent of the Baptist standard.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Reformed confession produced by the Westminster Assembly (1643–49), with its Larger and Shorter Catechisms — the high point of English-speaking Calvinism, beginning with Scripture and ordered by covenant. The 1689 Baptist Confession follows it closely, parting only on baptism and polity.

WESTMINSTER CONFESSION OF FAITH, noun. The confession framed by the Westminster Assembly of Divines, 1643–1649.

Accompanied by the Larger and Shorter Catechisms, a Directory for Worship, and a Form of Church Government.

Thoroughly Calvinistic and covenantal; it opens with the authority and sufficiency of Holy Scripture.

The Shorter Catechism teaches that man's chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy Him forever.

Closely followed by the 1689 London Baptist Confession, which departs on baptism, church, and magistrate.

Key Scripture

2 Tim 3:16 — "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness."

Jude 3 — "ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints."

1 Cor 10:31 — "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God."

Rom 11:36 — "For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen."

Modern Corruption

The modern church treats confessions as dusty relics or as chains on the conscience, prizing a vague "no creed but Christ" that in practice leaves every man his own pope; others revise the Confession to soften its hard doctrines of election and eternal punishment until it no longer says what its authors meant.

expand to see more

The first corruption is anti-confessionalism: the claim that a written confession competes with the Bible. But a confession does not stand over Scripture; it stands under it, openly declaring what the church believes the Scripture teaches, so that error has no place to hide. "No creed but the Bible" sounds humble and is often a cover for doctrinal drift, since every heretic also claims the Bible. The Westminster divines bound their confession explicitly to the Word as its only infallible rule.

The second corruption is revision that guts the substance: bodies that keep the name "Westminster" while striking out unconditional election, particular redemption, or eternal conscious punishment, and reading inclusive and affirming doctrine back into a document that knows nothing of it. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the original text, which is fixed and public; the corruption is in the churches that subscribe it with crossed fingers. The principle to recover is honest subscription — to confess what the words mean, or to stop calling oneself by them.

Hebrew Roots

From the Westminster Assembly (1643–49) + Latin confiteri (to acknowledge openly); a covenantal, Calvinistic confession ordered from Scripture to the last judgment.

Westminster — the Assembly met in the Jerusalem Chamber of the Abbey

Latin confiteri, to acknowledge or confess openly

Opens with Holy Scripture — its authority, sufficiency, and clarity

Covenantal structure: the covenant of works and the covenant of grace

Parent text of the 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith
